I think a lot of it is mentality and habit. My family raised me saying "you better finish all your food or you'll be hungry later", but I realize now just how messed up that view is. If I'm hungry later, I should just eat more then and not stuff myself now. That's how you stretch your stomach and overeat. I have to actively stop myself from having this mentality and remind myself that it's ok if I'm hungry later, no one will stop me from making myself more food now that I'm an adult.

I also watched two of my family members lose a ton of weight (150 lbs+) by exercising every day and heavily restricting their diet. It wasn't sustainable though because they were miserable the whole time. As soon as they lost the weight, they went right back to their old habits of eating huge portions and not exercising.

These are just my observations so take them for what they're worth. However, I'm easily maintaining a healthy weight now by going for a short jog in the morning (I'm sedentary the rest of the day) and eating healthy foods for most of my meals or small portions if it's something fairly unhealthy (like pizza). I'm never hungry, I never feel like I'm denying myself the food I want, and I don't feel guilty eating bacon and pizza because it's within the rules I've set for my "diet" to eat small amounts of them. I don't know that this would work for everyone, but I think this is a lot easier than trying to maintain a heavily restricted diet like no carbs and no unhealthy foods at all - which is what was recommended to my family and in many sources online.

The problem is that there is a feedback loop built into obesity and our society. Someone puts on weight: society shames them, they feel ashamed of their bodies, they console their shame with food and self-defeating attitudes. They put on more weight. They try to go to a gym and change it and everyone laughs at them for being fat at the gym, they buy healthier foods at the store and people give them weird looks like "yeah right, like you really eat this." Their shame builds, they console their shame with food and self-defeating attitudes. They put on more weight...

I have a feeling we'd see a lot more people successfully attaining and maintaining healthy weights if the focus of society moved away from shaming them, to positively encouraging them to make healthier decisions and helping them find ways to forgive themselves and keep trying when they backslide.
